Tip: In many Chinese businesses, building Guanxi (personal connections) is very important. People often spend time on meals and socializing before starting serious business discussions.

The concept of Mianzi (Face or reputation) is very important. In traditional settings, people often avoid direct criticism or a blunt 'no' in public to protect everyone's reputation. Subtle hints or private conversations are common.
Respect for age and seniority is common. In many situations, people wait for the most senior person to sit, speak, or eat first.
Time is often viewed flexibly. Meetings might start a bit late or run over schedule. This extra time is usually used to build personal relationships.
Building personal friendships is a key part of doing business. People often accept invitations for coffee or lunch, and schedules can be flexible.
Conversations often happen at a closer physical distance, and light touching (like a pat on the arm) is normal. Maintaining eye contact shows interest and respect.
Hospitality is very important. Accepting offers of tea or coffee is a good way to show respect. If invited to a home, bringing a small gift like high-quality sweets is a nice gesture.
Communication is often indirect to maintain harmony. A 'yes' might mean 'I hear you' rather than 'I agree.' People generally prefer to avoid direct public disagreement.
It is helpful to check prayer times when planning meetings. Dressing modestly (covering shoulders and knees) shows respect, especially in traditional areas or religious sites.

In many traditional companies, hierarchy is important. People often use formal titles (Sir/Madam) and decisions are usually made by senior leaders. However, modern startups and tech companies often have more relaxed, team-based structures.

To avoid causing offense, people often prefer not to say a direct 'no.' Instead, they might use phrases like 'I will try my best' or change the subject. It is helpful to pay attention to these subtle cues.
If eating with your hands, it is customary to use only the right hand. When dining with Hindu colleagues, it is respectful to avoid ordering beef, and with Muslim colleagues, avoid pork.
Taarof is a system of politeness. If a host or shopkeeper offers something or refuses payment, it is often polite to refuse or insist a few times. It is a way of showing respect.
Iranians are known for their great hospitality. Accepting food and drink helps build trust. However, if you must decline an offer, a polite and clear explanation is usually understood.
People pay close attention to tone and body language. To keep social harmony and respect, public disagreement or raising one's voice is usually avoided.
Business cards (meishi) are very important. Always give and receive them with both hands, look at the card carefully, and place it respectfully on the table.
Silence is often used for thinking and shows respect. It is normal to have a few seconds of pause after a question, so there is no need to rush to fill the silence.
In public spaces and on transport, people usually keep their voices low. Avoiding phone calls in shared spaces is a way to respect the group's peace and harmony (Wa).
Maintaining group harmony is very important. People usually avoid public criticism and handle disagreements privately and politely.
When planning meals, remember to check for Halal dietary rules. During the month of Ramadan, it is respectful not to eat, drink, or smoke in front of fasting colleagues during the day.
Using professional or honorific titles (like Dato' or Tan Sri) shows respect. Also, it is polite to point with your right thumb (with fingers folded under) instead of using your index finger.
Respect for age and status is important. It is polite to greet the oldest or most senior person first. Using professional titles (like Chief, Doctor, or Professor) shows great respect.
Building trust is a key part of business. Taking time for small talk and asking about family before discussing business is a normal and important practice.
Communication styles are often energetic, expressive, and passionate. This high energy and use of gestures show deep interest and engagement in the conversation.
In formal situations, people use the First Name and Patronymic (the father's name), along with the formal 'You' (Vy). Colleagues usually switch to the informal 'You' (Ty) only when invited to do so.

Building personal trust is essential, and major decisions are often made after socializing. Business dinners are a good opportunity to have meaningful conversations and build a strong working relationship.
Hierarchy is often respected in business. It is best to direct your main points to the most senior person in the room and follow the standard chain of command.
In US business culture, communication is usually direct and explicit. 'Yes' means yes, and 'No' means no. People generally prefer clear messages rather than having to guess intentions.
Punctuality is highly valued. Meetings usually start and end on time. If you are going to be late, it is important to let the other person know immediately.
The workplace often has a relaxed approach to hierarchy. It is common to use first names quickly and to respectfully discuss or challenge ideas, regardless of a person's job title.
